tip: ‘ellir’ is the impersonal can-form and needs no subject: ‘ni ellir newid’ = one cannot change.
With ‘ers’ (for), Welsh keeps the present tense to mean has been: ‘mae hi'n byw ... ers’ = she has lived for.
For as ... as, use ‘mor ... â’; ‘mor’ soft-mutates the adjective: ‘caled’ becomes ‘galed’. ‘mor galed â’ = as hard as.
Welsh needs no word for 'to' between two verbs: ‘dysgodd hi siarad’ = she learned to speak. ‘siarad’ stays plain.
‘tair’ is the feminine three, used with feminine nouns: ‘tair ystafell’ = three rooms. Masculine takes ‘tri’.
Reported questions keep statement order, with ‘mae’ straight after ‘pam’: ‘pam mae'r awyr yn las’ = why the sky is blue.
‘hoffwn i’ = I would like, and the next verb soft-mutates: ‘dysgu’ becomes ‘ddysgu’. ‘hoffwn i ddysgu’ = I'd like to learn.
Welsh has no verb for have: ‘mae pen tost gen i’ = there is a sore head with me, so I have a headache. ‘gen i’ = with me.
After ‘fy’ (my), ‘c’ nasal-mutates to ‘ngh’: ‘car’ becomes ‘nghar’. ‘fy nghar i’ = my car.
A past-tense verb's object soft-mutates: ‘cinio’ becomes ‘ginio’. ‘coginiodd Nerys ginio’ = Nerys cooked lunch.
Welsh links two nouns for 'of' with no separate word: ‘enw'r ci’ means the dog's name, literally name the-dog.
‘na’ turns a why-question negative and soft-mutates the verb: ‘dest’ becomes ‘ddest’ in ‘pam na ddest ti’ (why didn't you come).
‘dy’ (your) soft-mutates the next word and often echoes with ‘di’: ‘pen’ becomes ‘ben’ in ‘dy ben-blwydd di’ (your birthday).
After ‘beth’ (what) a verb soft-mutates: ‘digwyddodd’ becomes ‘ddigwyddodd’. ‘beth ddigwyddodd’ = what happened.
‘does dim’ means there is no and sits right before the noun: ‘does dim bara’ (there's no bread). It denies existence, not an action.
‘eisiau’ is the exception to the ‘yn’ rule: no ‘n’ comes before it, as in ‘dw i eisiau'r un glas’ (I want the blue one).
‘un’ before a feminine noun causes soft mutation: ‘merch’ becomes ‘ferch’ in ‘un ferch’ (one girl).
‘ar ôl’ placed after a noun means left or remaining: ‘dim tocynnau ar ôl’ (no tickets left).
‘alla i’ (can I) soft-mutates the verb that follows: ‘parcio’ becomes ‘barcio’ in ‘ble alla i barcio'r car’.
'this' and 'that' follow the noun in Welsh: ‘y gair hwn’ means this word, literally the word this.
‘mynd i’ plus a verb makes the future and soft-mutates it: ‘bwrw’ becomes ‘fwrw’ in ‘mynd i fwrw glaw’ (going to rain).
Use ‘tair’, not ‘tri’, for three before a feminine noun: ‘tair iaith’ (three languages).
The ‘-wch’ ending marks a formal or plural command: ‘cymerwch’ (take). The informal single-person form drops it: ‘cymer’.
‘ddim’ does the negating and follows the subject: ‘dyw hi ddim yn gwybod’ (she doesn't know), verb then subject then ‘ddim’.
The ‘-ir’ ending makes a verb impersonal, with no named doer: ‘disgwylir’ means is expected in ‘disgwylir i'r tywydd wella’.
Feminine nouns soft-mutate after ‘y’ or ‘'r’ (the): ‘cegin’ becomes ‘gegin’. ‘paentiodd e'r gegin’ = he painted the kitchen.
‘torth’ is feminine, so three is ‘tair’ not ‘tri’, here mutated to ‘dair’: ‘dair torth’ = three loaves.
The linking ‘yn’ soft-mutates the word after it, so ‘mantais’ turns into ‘fantais’ in ‘yn fantais’.
The ‘-ach’ ending makes an adjective comparative, more: ‘gryfach’ means stronger in ‘mae e'n gryfach’.
‘dylai’ means should or ought to: ‘dylai fe ymddiheuro’ = he should apologise. It has no plain past form.
